common_name: FlordaGrande Peach (Ultra-Low-Chill University of Florida Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; requires fewer than 100 chill hours, among the lowest of any named peach, so it sets fruit reliably even where winters barely dip below 60°F.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. FlordaGrande requires fewer than 100 chill hours, among the lowest of any named peach, so it sets fruit reliably even where winters barely dip below 60°F. It ripens very early, typically late April into May, on medium to large freestone fruit with orange-red skin and sweet, melting yellow flesh. Self-fertile and vigorous, it benefits from a hard summer prune to keep growth compact and from fruit thinning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy set. This is the standard recommendation for growers at the extreme low-chill end of zone 9-11 where even other Florida-bred peaches may fall short.
sources: UF/IFAS Horticultural Sciences Department Stone Fruit Breeding Program
UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

common_name: Earligrande Peach (Early Very-Low-Chill Yellow Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 275 chill hours, making it dependable for zone 8-9 gardens along the Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Earligrande needs only about 275 chill hours, making it a dependable early peach for zone 8-9 gardens along the Gulf Coast where higher-chill varieties fail to break dormancy evenly. Fruit ripens very early, usually mid to late April, with yellow, semi-clingstone flesh under mostly red-blushed skin. Trees are vigorous and heavy-bearing, so consistent hand thinning is needed to size the fruit and avoid limb stress.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

common_name: Flordadawn Peach (Early University of Florida Low-Chill Peach for North Florida)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; bred for roughly 350 chill hours, suiting the milder end of zone 8 through 9.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred by the University of Florida for roughly 350 chill hours, Flordadawn suits the milder end of zone 8 through 9 where standard peaches often set little or no fruit. It ripens in the early season with melting, semi-clingstone flesh and the mild sweet flavor typical of Florida's low-chill breeding lines. Like most Gulf South peaches it benefits from a dormant fungicide application and open-center pruning to manage the fungal pressure that comes with humid winters and springs.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs under 400 chill hours, performing well in zone 8-9 winters too mild for standard high-chill peaches.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. A California-bred freestone needing under 400 chill hours, Bonita performs well in zone 8-9 winters too mild for standard high-chill peaches. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed with a red blush, and has repeatedly scored among the top varieties in formal taste trials for its sweet, subacid flavor. It ripens in mid to late summer, later than most low-chill Gulf selections, which helps extend the home orchard's peach season. Self-fruitful and vigorous, a single tree sets a full crop without a pollinizer.

common_name: Rio Grande Peach (Texas-Bred Low-Chill Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; bred for roughly 400-500 chill hours, a dependable mid-season choice for the warmer half of zone 8 into zone 9.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred in Texas for roughly 400-500 chill hours, Rio Grande is a dependable mid-season choice for the warmer half of zone 8 into zone 9 where many standard peaches underperform. It produces large yellow freestone fruit with a red blush, ripening in June with rich, classic peach flavor. Self-fertile and heat-tolerant, it needs hot, sunny summers to size its fruit properly and can disappoint in cooler, cloudier growing seasons. A good mid-season companion to earlier ultra-low-chill selections for a longer harvest window.

common_name: Desert Gold Peach (Early Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 250 chill hours and blooms early, so site it sheltered from late cold snaps.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Introduced from Fresno, California in 1969 for about 250 chill hours, Desert Gold opens peach growing to the mildest winters of zone 8-9 where standard varieties will not set fruit. It is among the earliest peaches to ripen, often by late April to May, with medium semi-freestone fruit, yellow flesh, red-blushed skin, and a sweet, slightly tart flavor. Because it blooms early, a site sheltered from late cold snaps helps protect the blossoms from frost damage. Self-fruitful and heat-tolerant, it remains a long-standing standard recommendation for warm-winter home orchards.
